Definition

Antimicrobial stewardship is a coordinated set of interventions and strategies designed to optimise the use of antimicrobial agents — selecting the right drug, right dose, right route, right duration, and right indication — to maximise clinical cure while minimising adverse effects, toxicity, emergence of resistance, and healthcare costs. It is a core component of every healthcare facility's infection prevention & control (IPC) programme.

Goals / Aims

  • Optimise clinical outcomes — improved cure rates, reduced treatment failure, shorter length of stay.
  • Minimise unintended consequences — reduce antimicrobial resistance, Clostridioides difficile infection, adverse drug reactions, disruption of normal microbiome.
  • Reduce healthcare costs — minimise unnecessary or duplicate prescriptions; use cheaper equivalents when appropriate.
  • Preserve antimicrobial effectiveness for future use.

Core Elements of an Antimicrobial Stewardship Program (AMSP)

  1. Accountability — physician lead + pharmacist co-lead + microbiologist + infection control nurse.
  2. Drug expertise — clinical pharmacist.
  3. Key interventions
    • Pre-authorisation (restrictive) — certain antibiotics require approval before dispensing (e.g., meropenem, linezolid, colistin, tigecycline, echinocandins).
    • Prospective audit & feedback — review of ongoing therapy with recommendation to prescriber.
    • Formulary restriction — limited antibiotic availability.
    • Cycling & mixing — scheduled rotation to limit resistance.
    • Guidelines & care bundles — for empiric therapy of common infections (UTI, pneumonia, sepsis, SSI prophylaxis).
    • Dose optimisation — PK/PD-based dosing (extended infusion of β-lactams).
    • IV-to-oral conversion — switch when patient tolerates oral & clinically stable.
    • De-escalation — narrow spectrum once culture & sensitivity available.
    • Stop orders / automatic stop dates — review at 48–72 h and 5–7 days.
    • Duplicate therapy alerts — e.g., two drugs with overlapping spectra.
  4. Tracking & monitoring — antibiotic consumption (DDD/1000 patient-days); resistance patterns (antibiogram); C. difficile rates; clinical outcomes.
  5. Reporting — to prescribers, hospital administration, infection control committee.
  6. Education — regular training of medical, nursing, pharmacy staff.

Why AMSP Matters

  • Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) — >1.27 million deaths globally attributable to bacterial AMR in 2019 (Lancet); India has among the highest rates of multidrug-resistant organisms (MRSA, VRE, ESBL, CRE, CRAB, CRPA).
  • Misuse of antibiotics — ~50% of antibiotic prescriptions in hospitals are inappropriate (unnecessary, wrong drug, wrong dose, wrong duration).
  • Without effective antibiotics — chemotherapy, surgery, neonatal care, and transplantation become life-threatening.
  • WHO calls AMR one of the top 10 global public health threats.

Indian Context — ICMR AMSP

  • ICMR initiated AMSP network in 2017–2018; >150 hospitals enrolled.
  • Annual AMR surveillance reports — publish antibiograms.
  • "Red Line Campaign" — distinguishes prescription-only antibiotics (red line on packaging) from OTC.
  • National Action Plan on AMR (NAP-AMR, 2017–2021) — multi-sectoral "One Health" approach.

Clinical Pearl

The single most effective stewardship intervention is prospective audit & feedback — a pharmacist or ID physician reviews all antibiotic prescriptions after 48–72 h and recommends continuation, narrowing, switching to oral, or stopping. This reduces broad-spectrum antibiotic use by 20–30% without compromising outcomes. The second is pre-authorisation of last-resort antibiotics (carbapenems, colistin, linezolid, tigecycline) — approval by ID physician before dispensing. Always send cultures before starting antibiotics — this enables de-escalation from broad empiric to narrow targeted therapy within 48–72 h. The "Start Smart, Then Focus" approach (UK Department of Health) is the simplest bedside mnemonic — start with appropriate empiric therapy within 1 h of severe sepsis, then review at 48–72 h based on cultures and clinical response. Avoid antibiotics for viral upper respiratory infections — the single most common misuse of antibiotics in outpatient practice.
q1_0_2_1:
Definition

A superantigen (SAg) is a microbial exotoxin that bypasses normal antigen processing and activates a large fraction (5–30%) of T cells by binding directly to MHC class II outside the peptide groove and to the T-cell receptor Vβ chain outside the conventional antigen-binding site. This massive T-cell activation triggers a cytokine storm — the "exaggerated and inappropriate immune response".

Why the Response Is Exaggerated & Inappropriate

  1. Bypass of antigen processing — conventional antigen requires uptake, processing into peptides, loading on MHC-II groove, presentation to TCR. Only T cells with the specific complementary TCR (~1 in 10⁵–10⁶) are activated. SAg bypasses this — binds MHC-II & TCR Vβ directly without processing.
  2. Massive T-cell activation — each Vβ family is used by 2–20% of T cells; one SAg can activate 5–30% of all T cells (vs <0.001% for conventional antigen). This is 1000–100,000× more T cells than a normal immune response.
  3. Cytokine storm — activated T cells release IL-2, IFN-γ, TNF-β; macrophages (also activated by SAg) release IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-12, IL-8. Massive systemic inflammation → capillary leak, hypotension, multi-organ dysfunction, shock.
  4. Inappropriate — response is non-specific (does not target the pathogen that produced the SAg); damages host tissue; cytokine cascade is disproportionate to microbial threat; can be triggered by tiny amounts of SAg.
  5. T-cell anergy & deletion — after the initial burst, activated T cells undergo activation-induced cell death (AICD) or become anergic → immunosuppression; contributes to susceptibility to secondary infection.

Examples of Superantigens

  • Staphylococcus aureus — TSST-1 (toxic shock syndrome toxin-1; menstrual TSS); Enterotoxins A–E, G–U (food poisoning); SEB (bioterrorism agent).
  • Streptococcus pyogenes — SpeA, SpeC, SpeF, SMEZ (scarlet fever, streptococcal toxic shock syndrome).
  • Mycoplasma arthritidis — MAM (mouse arthritis).
  • Yersinia pseudotuberculosis — YPM.

Clinical Consequences

  • Toxic shock syndrome — high fever, hypotension, diffuse maculopapular rash with desquamation (palms/soles), multi-organ involvement; classically menstrual (tampon-associated TSST-1) or non-menstrual (post-surgical, burns).
  • Staphylococcal food poisoning — acute onset (2–6 h) of severe vomiting, cramps; self-limited.
  • Scarlet fever — fine sandpaper rash, fever, pharyngitis (SpeA).
  • Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome — severe invasive GAS infection; necrotising fasciitis.

Clinical Pearl

The defining hallmark of a superantigen is its ability to activate 5–30% of all T cells (vs <0.001% for conventional antigen) — by binding MHC-II and TCR Vβ outside the conventional antigen-binding sites. This explains the dramatic clinical presentations — toxic shock within hours with high fever, hypotension, diffuse rash, multi-organ failure. TSST-1 from S. aureus is the classic menstrual TSS pathogen (super-absorbent tampon — Rely brand — 1980 outbreak). Treatment — remove source (tampon, drain abscess); aggressive fluids; vasopressors; clindamycin (suppresses toxin synthesis); IVIG; vancomycin/oxacillin. The most common iatrogenic SAg-like syndrome is cytokine release syndrome (CRS) from CAR-T cell therapy — responds to tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R). Bacterial superantigens are heat-stable — SEB survives boiling for 30 min, so reheating contaminated food does not prevent food poisoning.
q1_0_2_12:
Pulse Polio Immunisation — Definition

Pulse polio immunisation is a mass vaccination strategy in which oral polio vaccine (OPV) is administered simultaneously to all children under 5 years of age in a country or region on a single day (or over a few days), repeated in pulses at intervals (typically 4–6 weeks), regardless of prior immunisation status. Launched in India in 1995, it is conducted as National Immunisation Days (NIDs) and Sub-National Immunisation Days (SNIDs).

Rationale — Same Day, Same Time, All Children

1. Replacement of Wild Poliovirus with Vaccine-Derived Virus

  • When all children receive OPV simultaneously, the vaccine virus temporarily replaces wild poliovirus in the environment & gut of children.
  • OPV virus replicates in the gut, is excreted in stool, spreads to unimmunised contacts (contact immunity) — effectively immunising even children missed by vaccination teams.
  • This establishes a "herd immunity barrier" — interrupts wild virus transmission chains.

2. Simultaneous Mucosal Immunity in All Children

  • OPV induces both humoral (IgG — protects against paralytic disease) and mucosal (IgA — prevents intestinal replication & transmission) immunity.
  • If vaccination is staggered, children vaccinated earlier could be re-infected by wild virus from unvaccinated children; simultaneous vaccination eliminates this gap.
  • Multiple doses are needed because OPV efficacy is ~30% per dose in India (vs 90%+ in developed countries) due to concurrent enteric infections, malnutrition, and interfering enteroviruses — so 5–10 doses are required for full protection.

3. Interruption of Wild Virus Transmission

  • By immunising all susceptible children on the same day, the susceptible pool is reduced below the threshold required for sustained transmission (R₀ < 1).
  • Wild poliovirus cannot find susceptible hosts → dies out.

4. Reaching the Unreached

  • Booth-based approach (4–5 booths per 1000 children) plus house-to-house "mop-up" rounds ensure high coverage (>95%).
  • Mobile teams for migrant populations, nomads, brick-kiln workers, construction sites.
  • Transit booths at railway stations, bus stands, markets, festivals.

5. Replacement Strategy — Why Same Day

  • If given on different days, the "vaccine virus window" in the gut is brief; wild virus can recolonise.
  • Same-day mass administration maintains a sustained "vaccine virus flood" in the community — displaces wild virus from circulation.
  • Pulses repeated 4–6 times per year maintain coverage above 95% — the level needed to interrupt transmission.

India's Success Story

  • India reported its last wild poliovirus case on 13 January 2011 (Howrah, West Bengal; type 1).
  • WHO certified India polio-free on 27 March 2014 (3 years without wild polio).
  • Strategy combined: routine immunisation + pulse polio + National Immunisation Days + mOPV1 (monovalent) + bivalent OPV (types 1 & 3) + intense Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance.

Switch from tOPV to bOPV (April 2016)

  • Global switch from trivalent OPV (types 1, 2, 3) to bivalent OPV (types 1, 3) — because type 2 was eradicated in 1999 but type 2 component of OPV caused most circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV2) outbreaks.
  • Single dose of IPV (inactivated polio vaccine) added to routine immunisation — provides type 2 immunity without risk of VDPV.
  • Endgame strategy: gradual withdrawal of OPV, switch to all-IPV schedule.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important reason for the "same day, same time" strategy is the replacement of wild poliovirus with vaccine virus in the community — simultaneous OPV administration floods the environment with attenuated vaccine virus, which outcompetes wild virus for intestinal receptors in unimmunised children, establishing herd immunity. India's polio eradication success — from 200,000 cases/year in the 1980s to zero in 2011 — is one of public health's greatest achievements, achieved through NIDs, mop-up rounds, mobile teams for migrant populations (Brick kiln workers in UP/Bihar were a major reservoir), and religious leader engagement (to counter rumours in Muslim communities). The new challenge is circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV) — especially type 2 — from continued OPV use; the global endgame is to switch entirely to IPV. India introduced fractional IPV (fIPV — 1/5th dose intradermally) at 6 & 14 weeks to stretch limited IPV supply. Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance remains the cornerstone — every case of AFP in a child <15 years must be reported & tested for poliovirus within 14 days (two stool samples 24–48 h apart).
q1_0_2_13:
Definition

Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are a family of evolutionary conserved pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) expressed on the surface or in endosomes of immune cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells, mast cells, epithelial cells) that recognise conserved microbial structures called pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). They are the sentinels of innate immunity, providing the first line of microbial recognition.

Named after the Drosophila Toll protein (essential for dorsal-ventral patterning & antifungal immunity); mammalian homologues discovered by Medzhitov & Janeway (1997). The discovery was awarded the 2011 Nobel Prize (Beutler & Hoffmann).

TLR Family — Types & Ligands

TLR Location Ligand (PAMP) Source organism
TLR1 (with TLR2)Cell surfaceTriacyl lipoproteinsBacteria, mycobacteria
TLR2 (with TLR1 or TLR6)Cell surfacePeptidoglycan, lipoteichoic acid, lipoproteins, lipoarabinomannan, zymosanGram-positive bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi
TLR3EndosomeDouble-stranded RNA (dsRNA)Viruses
TLR4 (with MD-2 & CD14)Cell surfaceLipopolysaccharide (LPS, endotoxin)Gram-negative bacteria; also RSV F protein, HSP60
TLR5Cell surfaceFlagellinMotile bacteria
TLR6 (with TLR2)Cell surfaceDiacyl lipoproteinsMycoplasma, Gram-positive
TLR7EndosomeSingle-stranded RNA (ssRNA), imiquimodViruses (influenza, HIV)
TLR8EndosomessRNA (guanosine/uridine-rich)Viruses
TLR9EndosomeUnmethylated CpG DNABacteria, DNA viruses (HSV)
TLR10Cell surfaceUnknown (likely lipoproteins)Bacteria

Signal Transduction & Function

  1. Ligand binding → TLR dimerisation (TLR2/1, TLR2/6, TLR4/MD2) → recruits adaptor proteins (MyD88, TIRAP, TRIF, TRAM).
  2. MyD88-dependent pathway (all TLRs except TLR3) — activates IRAK, TRAF6 → TAK1 → NF-κB & AP-1 → transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12).
  3. TRIF-dependent pathway (TLR3 & TLR4) — activates IRF3 → type I interferons (IFN-α, IFN-β) — antiviral response.
  4. Also activates MAPK, PI3K pathways → cell activation, survival, differentiation.

Roles of TLRs

  1. First-line antimicrobial defence — recognise PAMPs, trigger inflammation, activate innate immunity within minutes.
  2. Bridge to adaptive immunity — dendritic cell TLR activation upregulates co-stimulatory molecules (CD80, CD86) & MHC → efficient T cell priming; polarise Th1 (TLR4, TLR9), Th2, Th17 responses.
  3. Antiviral immunity — TLR3, 7, 8, 9 in endosomes detect viral nucleic acids → IFN-α/β production → antiviral state.
  4. Inflammation & sepsis — TLR4 recognises LPS; excessive activation → cytokine storm, septic shock.
  5. Wound healing & tissue repair — TLRs on epithelial cells.
  6. Recognition of DAMPs (Damage-Associated Molecular Patterns) — TLR2/4 recognise HMGB1, HSP60, HSP70 from necrotic cells → sterile inflammation.

Clinical Significance

  • TLR4 polymorphisms (Asp299Gly) — impaired LPS recognition; reduced sepsis risk but increased Gram-negative infection susceptibility; also reduced atherosclerosis risk.
  • Imiquimod (TLR7 agonist) — topical treatment for genital warts, basal cell carcinoma, actinic keratosis.
  • TLR agonists as adjuvants — CpG (TLR9) in vaccines; MPL (monophosphoryl lipid A, TLR4) in Cervarix HPV vaccine, Shingrix shingles vaccine.
  • TLR inhibitors — Eritoran (TLR4 inhibitor) — failed clinical trial for sepsis; ongoing research in autoimmune disease.
  • Autoimmunity — TLR7, TLR9 activation by self nucleic acids drives SLE (immune complexes containing DNA/RNA activate B cells & pDCs via TLR9/7).

Clinical Pearl

TLRs are the bridge between innate and adaptive immunity — without TLR signalling, dendritic cells cannot upregulate co-stimulatory molecules (CD80/86), and T cells become anergic rather than activated. This explains why alum (the traditional vaccine adjuvant) works partly through NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and why modern vaccines increasingly use TLR agonists (MPL in Cervarix, CpG in Heplisav-B) for stronger, more durable immune responses. TLR4 polymorphisms (Asp299Gly) are protective against Gram-negative sepsis but paradoxically increase susceptibility to Legionnaires' disease and respiratory infections. In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), immune complexes containing self-DNA/RNA activate TLR9 & TLR7 in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, driving type I interferon production — this is the basis for the "interferon signature" of SLE and the rationale for anti-IFN-α therapy (sifalimumab, anifrolumab). The TLR field has produced 2 Nobel Prizes — Hoffmann & Beutler (2011, physiology/medicine) for TLR activation of innate immunity; and Steinman (same year) for dendritic cell discovery.
q1_0_2_14:
Definition

A plasmid is a small, circular, double-stranded, extrachromosomal DNA molecule (1 kb to >1 Mb) that replicates independently of the bacterial chromosome. Plasmids carry non-essential but advantageous genes — including antibiotic resistance genes — that can be transferred between bacteria by conjugation, transformation, or transduction.

Types of Plasmids

  • R plasmid (Resistance plasmid) — carries antibiotic resistance genes. Most clinically important.
  • Col plasmid — produces colicins (bacteriocins) to kill competing bacteria.
  • Virulence plasmid — carries virulence factors (e.g., pColV in invasive E. coli; pTi in Agrobacterium tumefaciens).
  • Metabolic plasmid — catabolic genes (e.g., Tol plasmid in Pseudomonas for toluene degradation; Sym plasmid in Rhizobium for nitrogen fixation).
  • Fertility / F plasmid — enables conjugation (transfer of plasmid DNA between bacteria).

Structure of R Plasmid

  • RTF (Resistance Transfer Factor) — genes required for conjugation (tra operon — encodes sex pilus, conjugation machinery); origin of transfer (oriT); replication genes.
  • r-determinant (r-det) — antibiotic resistance genes; often present as transposons or integrons (mobile genetic elements that can hop between plasmids & chromosome).

Mechanisms of Antibiotic Resistance Mediated by Plasmids

1. Enzymatic Inactivation (most common)

  • β-lactamases — hydrolyse β-lactam ring of penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems.
    • TEM, SHV, CTX-M (ESBL — extended-spectrum β-lactamases) — confer resistance to third-generation cephalosporins.
    • KPC, NDM, VIM, IMP, OXA-48 (carbapenemases) — confer carbapenem resistance.
  • Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes — AAC (acetyltransferases), ANT (nucleotidyltransferases), APH (phosphotransferases) — modify aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin).
  • Chloramphenicol acetyltransferase (CAT) — inactivates chloramphenicol.
  • Erythromycin esterases — hydrolyse macrolides.

2. Efflux Pumps

  • Plasmid-encoded pumps actively expel antibiotics from bacterial cell — broad substrate specificity.
  • Examples — TetA, TetB (tetracycline efflux); MexAB-OprM in Pseudomonas (multiple drugs); Qac pumps (quaternary ammonium compounds).

3. Target Modification

  • erm gene — methylates 23S rRNA → macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin B (MLS) resistance.
  • dfr gene — alternative dihydrofolate reductase → trimethoprim resistance.
  • vanA, vanB — alter peptidoglycan precursor (D-Ala-D-Ala → D-Ala-D-Lac) → vancomycin resistance in enterococci.
  • mecA — altered PBP2a (penicillin-binding protein) → methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

4. Target Protection / Bypass

  • qnr — protects DNA gyrase from fluoroquinolones.
  • Alternative metabolic pathways — bypass drug target.

5. Reduced Permeability

  • Plasmid-encoded porin loss → reduced antibiotic entry.

Horizontal Gene Transfer — How Plasmids Spread Resistance

  1. Conjugation — most important clinically; F plasmid or R plasmid encodes sex pilus; donor cell (F+) transfers copy to recipient (F–); enables rapid spread of resistance within and between species (e.g., NDM-1 spread from Klebsiella to E. coli to other Enterobacterales).
  2. Transduction — bacteriophage-mediated transfer; less common.
  3. Transformation — uptake of free plasmid DNA from environment (e.g., Neisseria, Streptococcus).
  4. Transposons & integrons — mobile genetic elements that hop between plasmid and chromosome; carry resistance gene cassettes; integrons capture & express gene cassettes.

Examples of Clinically Important R Plasmids

  • pLVPK — Klebsiella; carries multiple resistance.
  • IncF, IncL/M, IncN, IncH, IncW, IncP — incompatibility groups; NDM-1 typically on IncL/M plasmids.
  • R100 — classic E. coli R plasmid (resistance to tetracycline, chloramphenicol, sulfa, streptomycin).
  • pKpQIL — KPC-carrying Klebsiella plasmid.

Clinical Significance

  • Plasmid-mediated resistance spreads rapidly within hospitals — single plasmid can transfer to multiple species.
  • NDM-1 (New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase) — first described in 2008 in a Swedish patient returning from New Delhi; plasmid-encoded; spread globally; confers resistance to all β-lactams including carbapenems; often co-carries resistance to fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, sulfonamides — leaving few treatment options (colistin, tigecycline, fosfomycin).
  • Plasmid-mediated resistance is the major driver of multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO) outbreaks in ICUs.

Clinical Pearl

The NDM-1 (New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase) story exemplifies plasmid-mediated resistance spread — encoded on a conjugative plasmid (IncL/M type), NDM-1 spread from Klebsiella pneumoniae to E. coli, Enterobacter, Citrobacter, and other Enterobacterales within years, appearing in hospitals worldwide. The gene is often flanked by transposons and integrons that facilitate its hopping between plasmids and into the chromosome, ensuring persistence. The plasmid typically co-carries 6–10 other resistance genes (for fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides, sulfonamides, rifampin) — making the host organism pandrug-resistant (PDR), susceptible only to colistin (and increasingly colistin-resistant strains are appearing via the mcr-1 plasmid gene). This is why antibiotic stewardship, infection control, and surveillance are inseparable — a single NDM-1 carrier can seed an entire ICU with multidrug-resistant organisms within days through plasmid conjugation. Plasmids are why antibiotic resistance is here to stay — they spread faster than new antibiotics can be developed. The future belongs to non-antibiotic strategies — phage therapy, anti-virulence agents, microbiome restoration, and vaccines.
q1_0_2_5:
Introduction

IgG is the most abundant serum immunoglobulin (75–80% of total Ig; 8–16 mg/mL), the principal antibody of the secondary immune response, and the only Ig that crosses the placenta.

Structure

  • Y-shaped monomer, 150 kDa — 2 heavy (γ) chains + 2 light (κ or λ) chains linked by disulfide bonds.
  • Heavy chain (γ) — 4 domains: VH + Cγ1, Cγ2, Cγ3; lacks hinge between Cγ2 & Cγ3.
  • Hinge region — flexible proline-rich segment between Cγ1 & Cγ2; allows Fab arms to open & bind epitopes at variable distances; susceptible to papain & pepsin.
  • Enzymatic cleavage
    • Papain → 2 Fab (antigen-binding, monovalent) + 1 Fc (effector functions).
    • Pepsin → 1 F(ab')₂ (bivalent) + small pFc' fragments.
  • Fab — VH + VL; contains paratope (CDR1–3) that binds epitope.
  • Fc — Cγ2 + Cγ3; mediates complement activation (C1q binds Cγ2) & Fcγ receptor binding (Cγ3).
  • Subclasses (4) — IgG1 (66%), IgG2 (23%, polysaccharide antigens — encapsulated bacteria), IgG3 (7%, strongest complement), IgG4 (4%, chronic antigen exposure, IgG4-related disease).
  • Half-life — 21 days (longest of all Igs; due to FcRn-mediated recycling).

Functions

  1. Neutralisation — blocks viral/bacterial attachment & toxin action.
  2. Opsonisation — Fc binds FcγRI (CD64) on phagocytes → enhanced phagocytosis.
  3. Complement activation (classical pathway) — C1q binds Fc of adjacent IgG molecules → C3b → MAC lysis.
  4. ADCC — FcγRIII (CD16) on NK cells binds Fc of IgG-coated target → perforin/granzyme-mediated killing.
  5. Transplacental transfer — FcRn (neonatal Fc receptor) in placental syncytiotrophoblast actively transports IgG to fetal circulation; provides passive immunity to neonate for first 6 months.
  6. Half-life extension — FcRn in endothelial cells recycles IgG, protecting from lysosomal degradation.
  7. Immune complex clearance — IgG-antigen complexes bind RBC CR1; transported to liver/spleen.
  8. Feedback inhibition — IgG-antigen complex binds FcγRIIb on B cells → inhibits further B-cell activation.

Clinical Significance

  • Maternal IgG protects neonate for 6 months.
  • Used as therapeutic IVIG for immunodeficiency, ITP, Guillain-Barré, Kawasaki.
  • IgG2 subclass deficiency — recurrent sinopulmonary infection with encapsulated bacteria.
  • IgG4-related disease — autoimmune pancreatitis, Mikulicz syndrome, Riedel thyroiditis.
  • Most therapeutic monoclonal antibodies are IgG1 or IgG4 (trastuzumab, rituximab, infliximab).

Clinical Pearl

IgG is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta — mediated by FcRn (Brambell receptor). This explains why maternal IgG anti-D (Rh) causes haemolytic disease of the newborn — maternal anti-Rh IgG crosses to fetal circulation and destroys Rh+ fetal RBCs. The same mechanism is exploited therapeutically: anti-D immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) given to Rh-negative mothers at 28 weeks & within 72 h of delivery clears fetal Rh+ cells before maternal B cells are sensitised. Because IgG has the longest half-life (21 d), it is the basis for monoclonal antibody therapy and IVIG replacement therapy (400–600 mg/kg every 3–4 weeks).
q1_0_2_15:
Definition

Enriched media are culture media supplemented with additional nutrients (blood, serum, egg, yeast extract, haemin, vitamin K, growth factors) to support the growth of fastidious microorganisms — bacteria or fungi that require complex growth factors and cannot grow on simple media like nutrient agar.

Fastidious organisms need:

  • Vitamins — NAD (V factor), hemin (X factor), vitamin K, vitamin B12, folate.
  • Amino acids, nucleotides.
  • Blood — for haemin, iron, growth factors.
  • CO₂ (capnophiles — Streptococcus, Neisseria gonorrhoeae).
  • Serum proteins, lipids.

Examples (2 detailed)

1. Blood Agar

  • Composition — nutrient agar base (peptone, beef extract, NaCl, agar, water, pH 7.4) + 5–10% defibrinated sheep/horse blood.
  • Why enriched — provides X factor (hemin), V factor (NAD — partially), iron, amino acids, vitamins; supports growth of fastidious organisms — Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Neisseria, Corynebacterium, Listeria, enterococci, pneumococci.
  • Preparation — autoclave base; cool to 45–50 °C; add sterile defibrinated blood; pour plates.
  • Haemolysis patterns
    • α-haemolysis — partial; greenish discolouration (methaemoglobin) — S. pneumoniae, viridans strep.
    • β-haemolysis — complete; clear zone — S. pyogenes, S. agalactiae, S. aureus.
    • γ-haemolysis — no change — Enterococcus, CoNS.
  • Special tests — Optochin (S. pneumoniae), Bacitracin (S. pyogenes), CAMP (S. agalactiae), Satellitism (Haemophilus).

2. Chocolate Agar

  • Composition — blood agar heated to 70–80 °C until colour changes to brown ("chocolate"). Heating lyses RBCs, releasing intracellular X (hemin) & V factor (NAD — normally intracellular in RBCs).
  • Why enriched — supports growth of more fastidious organisms than blood agar; especially those needing both X & V factors.
  • Organisms that grow on chocolate agar but NOT blood agar
    • Haemophilus influenzae (requires X + V).
    • Neisseria gonorrhoeae & N. meningitidis (require V factor; capnophilic — 5% CO₂).
    • Moraxella catarrhalis.
  • Uses — sputum (H. influenzae); urethral/cervical swab (N. gonorrhoeae — Thayer-Martin selective); CSF (meningitis); eye swab (H. aegyptius).
  • Variants — Thayer-Martin (chocolate + vancomycin + colistin + nystatin — selective for pathogenic Neisseria); NYC medium; Martin-Lewis; GC-Lect.

Other Enriched Media (brief)

  • Loeffler's serum slope — serum + egg + glucose — for Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
  • Lowenstein-Jensen — egg + malachite green + glycerol — for M. tuberculosis.
  • Todd-Hewitt broth — for Streptococcus.
  • Trypticase soy agar (TSA) / Brain heart infusion (BHI) — general-purpose enriched.
  • Cooked meat broth (Robertson's) — enriched + anaerobic — for Clostridium.
  • Fildes medium — peptic digest of blood — for H. influenzae.

Difference from Related Media

Type Function Example
Simple / basalSupports non-fastidious organismsNutrient agar, peptone water
EnrichedSupplemented to grow fastidiousBlood agar, chocolate agar
Enrichment brothSelective for pathogen (inhibits competitors)Selenite F (Salmonella), Alkaline peptone water (Vibrio)
SelectiveAntibiotics inhibit some, favour othersMacConkey, TCBS, LJ
DifferentialDistinguishes by colour/morphologyMacConkey (LF/NLF), Blood agar (haemolysis)

Clinical Pearl

The single most important practical lesson: chocolate agar is needed for suspected Haemophilus influenzae and Neisseria infections — these organisms will not grow on blood agar because they require V factor (NAD) which is intracellular in RBCs and only released when blood is heated. For a febrile child with meningitis, always plate CSF on both blood agar & chocolate agar (in 5% CO₂). For suspected gonorrhoea, use Thayer-Martin selective chocolate agar — non-selective chocolate agar will be overgrown by normal flora.
q1_0_2_16:
Definition

Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) — invented by Kary Mullis (1983; Nobel Prize 1993) — is an in vitro enzymatic method for exponential amplification of a specific DNA sequence by repeated cycles of denaturation, primer annealing, and extension, using a thermostable DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus).

Principle — Three-Step Cycle

  1. Denaturation — heat to 94–95 °C for 30 sec → separates double-stranded DNA into single strands.
  2. Annealing — cool to 50–65 °C for 30 sec → sequence-specific primers (forward & reverse) bind (hybridise) to complementary sequences flanking the target.
  3. Extension — heat to 72 °C for 1 min → Taq polymerase extends primers, synthesising new DNA strand complementary to template, using free dNTPs.

Each cycle doubles the target DNA; 30 cycles produce ~10⁹ copies (2³⁰) from a single template.

Components

  • Template DNA (sample — blood, tissue, CSF, sputum).
  • Sequence-specific primers (forward + reverse, 20–30 bp).
  • Thermostable DNA polymerase (Taq, Pfu, Tth — has 5'→3' polymerase activity; lacks 3'→5' exonuclease proofreading in Taq).
  • dNTPs (dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP).
  • Mg²⁺ (cofactor).
  • Buffer (Tris-HCl, KCl, pH 8.3).

Types of PCR

1. Conventional / End-point PCR

  • Detects product at end of cycling by gel electrophoresis (agarose + ethidium bromide).
  • Qualitative (presence/absence).
  • Limit — cannot quantify; contamination risk; post-PCR processing.

2. Real-time / Quantitative PCR (qPCR)

  • Monitors amplification in real-time using fluorescent dyes or probes.
  • SybR Green — binds dsDNA; non-specific.
  • TaqMan probe — sequence-specific; hydrolysis probe with fluorescent reporter & quencher; fluorescence emitted when probe cleaved.
  • FRET probes (HybProbe) — two probes; fluorescence resonance energy transfer.
  • Molecular beacons — hairpin probes.
  • Quantitative — Ct (cycle threshold) value; lower Ct = higher initial template.
  • Faster; closed-tube (low contamination); quantitative; sensitive.

3. Reverse Transcription PCR (RT-PCR)

  • For RNA targets — first convert RNA to cDNA using reverse transcriptase (MMLV, AMV); then PCR amplify.
  • Used for RNA viruses — HIV, HCV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, dengue; mRNA expression studies.

4. Multiplex PCR

  • Multiple primer pairs in one reaction → amplifies multiple targets simultaneously.
  • Examples — respiratory virus panel (BioFire FilmArray — 20+ pathogens); STI panel (CT/NG/MG/TV); meningitis/encephalitis panel; gastrointestinal panel.

5. Nested PCR

  • Two rounds of PCR — outer primers, then inner (nested) primers; increased sensitivity & specificity.
  • Used for low-copy targets — HIV proviral DNA, Toxoplasma in CSF.
  • Limit — high contamination risk.

6. Reverse Line Blot / PCR-RFLP

  • PCR + restriction enzyme digestion + electrophoresis — detects mutations; HLA typing; HPV genotyping.

7. Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP)

  • Isothermal (60–65 °C, no thermal cycler); uses Bst polymerase with strand displacement activity; 4–6 primers.
  • Field-deployable; result in 30–60 min; readout by turbidity, fluorescence, or colour change.
  • Used for TB (TB-LAMP), malaria, COVID-19, dengue.

8. Digital PCR (dPCR / ddPCR)

  • Sample partitioned into thousands of droplets; PCR in each; counts positive partitions.
  • Absolute quantification without standard curve; high precision.
  • Used for rare allele detection, copy number variation, liquid biopsy (circulating tumour DNA).

9. Other Types

  • Hot-start PCR — polymerase activated only at high temperature; reduces non-specific amplification.
  • Touchdown PCR — annealing temperature decreases over cycles; increases specificity.
  • Asymmetric PCR — generates single-stranded DNA (sequencing probes).
  • Colony PCR — directly from bacterial colony.
  • Quantitative RT-PCR (RT-qPCR) — RT-PCR + qPCR; quantifies RNA expression; gold standard for SARS-CoV-2 viral load.
  • Whole Genome Amplification (MDA, WGA) — for single-cell genomics.

Diagnostic Applications

Field Examples
Infectious diseaseTB (CBNAAT/Xpert MTB-RIF — detects rifampicin resistance); HIV (viral load, infant diagnosis); HCV (viral load, genotyping); HBV (viral load); SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR; dengue; influenza; HSV encephalitis (CSF); CMV; EBV; malaria; leishmaniasis; Toxoplasma; syphilis (PCR of lesion); gonorrhoea/chlamydia; pertussis; Mycoplasma
GeneticsHLA typing; triplet repeat disorders (Huntington, fragile X); sickle cell (HbS); thalassaemia mutations; cystic fibrosis; Duchenne; breast cancer (BRCA1/2); pharmacogenomics (CYP2D6, CYP2C19, HLA-B*5701)
OncologyBCR-ABL (CML); PML-RARA (APL); JAK2 V617F (MPN); BRAF V600E (melanoma); KRAS (colon cancer); EGFR (lung cancer); HER2; liquid biopsy (ctDNA)
ForensicDNA fingerprinting (STR profiling); paternity testing; identification of remains; crime scene analysis
Antibiotic resistancemecA (MRSA); vanA/B (VRE); blaCTX-M (ESBL); blaKPC, blaNDM, blaOXA-48 (CRE); rpoB (rifampin resistance in TB); katG/inhA (isoniazid); gyrA (fluoroquinolone)
Food & waterDetection of Salmonella, E. coli O157, Listeria, GMO screening

Advantages

  • High sensitivity (detects <10 copies); high specificity.
  • Rapid (2–4 h); can be automated.
  • Can detect non-cultivable or fastidious organisms.
  • Can detect antimicrobial resistance genes.
  • Quantitative (qPCR).

Limitations

  • Cannot distinguish live vs dead organisms (detects DNA from both).
  • Contamination risk (carryover from previous amplifications).
  • Inhibitors in sample (haemoglobin, heparin).
  • Requires expensive equipment & trained personnel.
  • False positives due to contamination; false negatives due to inhibitors or mutations in primer binding sites.

Clinical Pearl

The most widely used PCR in Indian clinical microbiology is CBNAAT (Cartridge-Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test) — Xpert MTB/RIF (Cepheid) — detects M. tuberculosis DNA & rifampicin resistance (rpoB gene mutations) in 2 hours from sputum. This revolutionised TB diagnosis — replaced sputum smear microscopy (sensitivity 50–60%) with sensitivity 90%+ and simultaneous drug resistance detection. The COVID-19 pandemic made RT-PCR a household term — it remains the gold standard for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis (E, N, RdRp genes; Orf1a/b). For HCV, HCV RNA PCR is the test of cure — target undetectable at 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12). HIV-1 DNA PCR on dried blood spot is the test of choice for infant diagnosis (maternal IgG confounds antibody tests until 18 months). The future is point-of-care multiplex PCR panels — BioFire FilmArray respiratory panel (20+ pathogens in 1 hour), gastrointestinal panel (22 pathogens), meningitis/encephalitis panel (14 pathogens) — these transform clinical decision-making at the bedside.

Introduction

Anaerobic bacteria require reduced oxygen tension (or absence of O₂) for growth — they cannot grow in 21% O₂ (atmospheric). Important human pathogens include Clostridium spp. (C. perfringens, C. tetani, C. botulinum, C. difficile), Bacteroides fragilis, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Actinomyces, Propionibacterium acnes.

Methods of Anaerobic Culture

1. Anaerobic Jar (McIntosh & Filde's jar) — Most commonly used

  • Principle — H₂ + O₂ → H₂O (catalysed by palladium catalyst) removes O₂ from sealed jar.
  • Procedure
    1. Inoculated plates placed inside jar.
    2. Place gas-generating sachet (GasPak — sodium borohydride + citric acid + cobalt chloride; produces H₂ & CO₂ on adding water).
    3. Palladium catalyst (in lid) catalyses H₂ + O₂ → H₂O.
    4. Seal jar; incubate at 37 °C for 48 h.
    5. Methylene blue indicator strip (blue in O₂, colourless in anaerobic) confirms anaerobiosis.
  • Indicators
    • Methylene blue — blue (oxidised, O₂ present) → colourless (reduced, anaerobic).
    • Resazurin — pink (O₂) → colourless.
  • Limit — does not achieve strict anaerobiosis (some O₂ remains).

2. Anaerobic Chamber / Glove Box (Coy, Whitley)

  • Largest & most sophisticated method — sealed chamber filled with gas mixture (N₂ 85%, H₂ 5%, CO₂ 10%); operator handles cultures through gloves.
  • Strictest anaerobiosis; allows processing of specimens & subculture without O₂ exposure.
  • Expensive; needs continuous gas supply.

3. Anaerobic Bags / Pouches (GasPak EZ)

  • Single-plate system — plate + gas-generating sachet sealed in transparent pouch.
  • Convenient for small labs; no jar needed; individual plate incubation.
  • Result read directly without opening.

4. Robertson's Cooked Meat (RCM) Broth

  • Liquid medium containing minced cooked meat (beef heart) — provides nutrients, reducing agents (sulphydryl groups in cysteine, glutathione), anaerobic environment at the bottom.
  • Meat particles act as reducing agents (maintain low Eh).
  • For Clostridium — gas production, "stormy fermentation" in milk (C. perfringens); digestion of meat particles (proteolytic species).
  • Useful for recovery from blood cultures & wound swabs.

5. Thioglycollate Broth (Brewer's)

  • Sodium thioglycollate — reducing agent (lowers Eh); maintains anaerobic conditions at the bottom of tube.
  • Methylene blue indicator — pink at top (O₂), colourless at bottom.
  • Used for sterility testing of biological products; blood culture.

6. Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) with Vitamin K & Hemin

  • Enriched broth for fastidious anaerobes.
  • Used in automated blood culture systems (BACTEC, BacT/ALERT) with anaerobic bottles.

7. PRAS (Pre-Reduced Anaerobically Sterilised) Media

  • Media prepared, poured, sterilised, and stored under anaerobic conditions throughout — never exposed to O₂.
  • Roll tubes (Hungate tubes) — agar slants in tubes flushed with O₂-free gas.
  • For fastidious anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium).

8. Special Media for Anaerobes

  • Brucella blood agar — enriched with vitamin K, hemin; for Bacteroides, Prevotella.
  • Bacteroides bile esculin agar (BBE) — selective for B. fragilis group (bile-tolerant, esculin hydrolysis).
  • Kanamycin-vancomycin laked blood agar (KVLB) — selective for Prevotella, Bacteroides.
  • Egg yolk agar (Nagler) — for Clostridium perfringens (lecithinase positive — opacity around colonies; inhibited by anti-α-toxin = positive Nagler reaction).
  • Cycloserine-cefoxitin-fructose agar (CCFA) — selective for C. difficile.
  • TPYG agar — Trypticase phytone yeast extract glucose.

9. Automated Anaerobic Blood Culture Systems

  • BACTEC (BD), BacT/ALERT (bioMérieux) — continuous monitoring; anaerobic bottles with reducing agents; alarm when CO₂ produced by growth detected.

Specimen Collection for Anaerobes

  • Avoid contamination with normal flora — collect from sites normally sterile.
  • Use aspirate (syringe) rather than swab where possible — aspirate in anaerobic transport tube.
  • Transport media — Stuart's, Cary-Blair, Amies; or PRAS tubes.
  • Rapid transport to lab (<2 h); refrigeration kills some anaerobes.
  • Sites acceptable — deep wound aspirate, blood, CSF, pleural fluid, peritoneal fluid, deep abscess, tissue biopsy, transtracheal aspirate.
  • Sites NOT acceptable (contaminated with normal flora) — throat, sputum (unless bronchial wash), stool (except C. difficile), vaginal swab (except culdocentesis), urethra, superficial wound.

Identification

  • Gram stain morphology — Gram-positive bacilli (Clostridium, Actinomyces, Propionibacterium); Gram-negative bacilli (Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium); Gram-positive cocci (Peptostreptococcus); Gram-negative cocci (Veillonella).
  • Colonial morphology, pigment production (Prevotella melaninogenica — black colonies), haemolysis, fluorescence under UV (B. fragilis — red; Prevotella — brick-red).
  • Biochemical tests — catalase, indole, nitrate, bile tolerance, sugar fermentation.
  • MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry — rapid identification (minutes).
  • 16S rRNA gene sequencing — gold standard for difficult identifications.
  • Molecular tests — PCR for toxin genes (C. perfringens alpha toxin; C. difficile toxin A/B; C. botulinum neurotoxin A/B/E/F; C. tetani tetanospasmin).

Clinical Pearl

The single most important clinical clue to anaerobic infection is foul-smelling (fetid) pus — caused by volatile short-chain fatty acids produced by anaerobic metabolism. Other clues — gas in tissue (gas gangrene — C. perfringens), tissue necrosis, location near mucosal surfaces (oral, GI, GU tract infections), infection after bite wounds (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Prevotella + Pasteurella), aspiration pneumonia (Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium), intra-abdominal abscess (B. fragilis), pelvic inflammatory disease (Bacteroides, Prevotella), brain abscess (Peptostreptococcus, Bacteroides, Fusobacterium), infected diabetic foot ulcer (polymicrobial with anaerobes). Always suspect anaerobes when: (1) foul smell, (2) gas in tissue, (3) necrosis, (4) failure to grow on aerobic culture with pus on Gram stain, (5) infection near mucosa, (6) bite wound, (7) post-abdominal/pelvic surgery. Empirical antibiotics covering anaerobes — metronidazole (drug of choice for Bacteroides, Clostridium); clindamycin (anaerobic cocci, Actinomyces); carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem); β-lactam + β-lactamase inhibitor (ampicillin-sulbactam, piperacillin-tazobactam); moxifloxacin; tigecycline. C. difficile requires oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin (not metronidazole first-line anymore per 2021 IDSA guidelines).

Definition

Mutation is a stable, heritable change in the nucleotide sequence of the genome. It can occur spontaneously (errors in DNA replication, tautomeric shifts, deamination, depurination) or be induced by mutagens (physical — UV, X-ray; chemical — nitrous acid, alkylating agents, base analogues; biological — transposons, viral integration). Rate: ~10⁻⁶ to 10⁻¹⁰ per gene per generation in bacteria.

Types of Mutation

1. Point Mutation — Single nucleotide change

  • Transition — purine → purine (A↔G) or pyrimidine → pyrimidine (C↔T). Most common (70%).
  • Transversion — purine → pyrimidine or vice versa (A↔C, A↔T, G↔C, G↔T). Less common.

By Functional Consequence

  • Silent (synonymous) — codon changes but encodes same amino acid (codon degeneracy); no phenotypic change.
  • Missense — codon changes to encode different amino acid. Conservative (similar aa — mild) or non-conservative (dissimilar — severe). Example — HbS (sickle cell): Glu→Val at position 6 of β-globin (GAG→GTG transversion).
  • Nonsense — codon changes to a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) → premature termination → truncated, usually non-functional protein. Example — Duchenne muscular dystrophy (dystrophin truncation).
  • Stop-loss — stop codon → sense codon → elongated protein.

2. Frameshift Mutation

  • Insertion or deletion of nucleotides in a number not divisible by 3 → shifts reading frame → different amino acid sequence downstream → premature stop codon → non-functional protein.
  • Example — Tay-Sachs disease (HEXA 4-bp insertion); Hb Wayne.

3. Insertion / Deletion (InDel)

  • Small (1–1000 bp) — frameshift if not multiple of 3.
  • Large — deletion of entire gene/exon. Example — α-thalassaemia (--SEA deletion); Duchenne (dystrophin exon deletion).

4. Dynamic / Expansion Mutation (Trinucleotide Repeat)

Expansion of unstable trinucleotide repeat beyond threshold during meiosis — causes anticipation. Examples:

  • Huntington disease — CAG in HTT (≥36 repeats).
  • Fragile X — CGG in FMR1 (>200 repeats).
  • Myotonic dystrophy — CTG in DMPK (>50 repeats).
  • Friedreich ataxia — GAA in FXN (>66 repeats).
  • Spinocerebellar ataxias — CAG in various genes.

5. Copy Number Variation (CNV)

  • Duplication or deletion of large segments (>1 kb). Examples — Hb Lepore (δβ fusion); CMT1A (PMP22 duplication).

6. Chromosomal Mutations

  • Numerical — aneuploidy (trisomy 21 Down, 18 Edward, 13 Patau, XXY Klinefelter, X Turner); polyploidy (lethal in humans).
  • Structural
    • Deletion (5p- Cri-du-chat, 22q11.2 DiGeorge).
    • Duplication.
    • Inversion (Factor VIII intron 22 inversion in Haemophilia A).
    • Translocation — Philadelphia t(9;22) in CML (BCR-ABL); t(14;18) follicular lymphoma (BCL2); t(8;14) Burkitt lymphoma (MYC).
    • Ring chromosome, isochromosome.

7. Conditional / Reversible

  • Suppressor mutation — second mutation restores phenotype.
  • Back mutation — reversion to wild-type.

By Effect on Phenotype

  • Loss-of-function — reduced/abolished activity; recessive (PKU, albinism).
  • Gain-of-function — new/enhanced activity; dominant (Huntington, achondroplasia FGFR3).
  • Dominant-negative — mutant interferes with wild-type (Marfan, p53).

By Origin

  • Germ-line — heritable (BRCA1 in familial breast cancer).
  • Somatic — not heritable; causes cancer (TP53 in lung cancer).

Clinical Significance

  1. Genetic diseases — sickle cell anaemia, thalassaemia, cystic fibrosis (ΔF508), Huntington, Duchenne, haemophilia A, phenylketonuria, Tay-Sachs, fragile X, hereditary cancer syndromes (BRCA1/2, Lynch, Li-Fraumeni).
  2. Cancer — somatic mutations drive oncogenesis (TP53, KRAS, EGFR, BRAF, BCR-ABL, MYC); guide targeted therapy (EGFR mutation → erlotinib; BCR-ABL → imatinib; BRAF V600E → vemurafenib; BRCA1/2 → PARP inhibitor olaparib).
  3. Pharmacogenomics — CYP2D6 polymorphisms affect codeine metabolism; HLA-B*5701 predisposes to abacavir hypersensitivity; TPMT variants affect thiopurine metabolism; G6PD deficiency — haemolysis with primaquine, sulfonamides, fava beans.
  4. Antibiotic resistance — mutations in rpoB (rifampicin resistance in TB), gyrA (fluoroquinolone resistance), katG & inhA (isoniazid), rpsL & rrs (streptomycin); HBV polymerase mutations (lamivudine, entecavir resistance); HIV reverse transcriptase & protease mutations.
  5. Forensic & paternity — DNA fingerprinting (STR profiling).
  6. Prenatal & carrier diagnosis — chorionic villus sampling, amniocentesis; preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD).
  7. Evolution & biodiversity — mutations are the raw material for natural selection.
  8. Immune diversity — V(D)J recombination in T & B cell receptors generates >10¹⁰ unique specificities.

Mutagens (Inducers)

  • Base analogues — 5-bromouracil, 2-aminopurine.
  • Alkylating agents — EMS, MNNG, nitrogen mustard.
  • Deaminating agents — nitrous acid (HNO₂) — converts adenine → hypoxanthine (pairs with C), cytosine → uracil.
  • Intercalating agents — acridine orange, proflavin, ethidium bromide — frameshift.
  • UV radiation — thymine dimers (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer).
  • Ionising radiation — X-ray, gamma-ray — single & double-strand breaks.

DNA Repair Mechanisms

  • Direct repair — photolyase (bacteria); O⁶-methylguanine methyltransferase (MGMT).
  • Base excision repair (BER) — for deaminated/oxidised bases.
  • Nucleotide excision repair (NER) — for bulky lesions; defective in xeroderma pigmentosum.
  • Mismatch repair (MMR) — defective in Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer).
  • Double-strand break repair — homologous recombination (BRCA1/2); non-homologous end joining (NHEJ).

Clinical Pearl

The Ames test uses his⁻ Salmonella typhimurium to detect mutagens — if a chemical induces reverse mutation to his⁺, the bacteria grow on histidine-free medium → mutagen identified. ~85% of known human carcinogens are mutagens in the Ames test. In clinical practice, the most useful application is targeted cancer therapy based on mutation profile: EGFR mutation in lung adenocarcinoma → erlotinib/gefitinib; BCR-ABL in CML → imatinib; BRAF V600E in melanoma → vemurafenib; BRCA1/2 in breast/ovarian cancer → PARP inhibitor (olaparib); KRAS G12C → sotorasib. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) of tumours is now standard of care. Hotspot mutations (KRAS codon 12, TP53 codon 248, BRAF V600) recur across cancer types because they occur in critical functional domains.

Definition

Antimicrobial stewardship is a coordinated set of interventions and strategies designed to optimise the use of antimicrobial agents — selecting the right drug, right dose, right route, right duration, and right indication — to maximise clinical cure while minimising adverse effects, toxicity, emergence of resistance, and healthcare costs. It is a core component of every healthcare facility's infection prevention & control (IPC) programme.

Goals / Aims

  • Optimise clinical outcomes — improved cure rates, reduced treatment failure, shorter length of stay.
  • Minimise unintended consequences — reduce antimicrobial resistance, Clostridioides difficile infection, adverse drug reactions, disruption of normal microbiome.
  • Reduce healthcare costs — minimise unnecessary or duplicate prescriptions; use cheaper equivalents when appropriate.
  • Preserve antimicrobial effectiveness for future use.

Core Elements of an Antimicrobial Stewardship Program (AMSP)

  1. Accountability — physician lead + pharmacist co-lead + microbiologist + infection control nurse.
  2. Drug expertise — clinical pharmacist.
  3. Key interventions
    • Pre-authorisation (restrictive) — certain antibiotics require approval before dispensing (e.g., meropenem, linezolid, colistin, tigecycline, echinocandins).
    • Prospective audit & feedback — review of ongoing therapy with recommendation to prescriber.
    • Formulary restriction — limited antibiotic availability.
    • Cycling & mixing — scheduled rotation to limit resistance.
    • Guidelines & care bundles — for empiric therapy of common infections (UTI, pneumonia, sepsis, SSI prophylaxis).
    • Dose optimisation — PK/PD-based dosing (extended infusion of β-lactams).
    • IV-to-oral conversion — switch when patient tolerates oral & clinically stable.
    • De-escalation — narrow spectrum once culture & sensitivity available.
    • Stop orders / automatic stop dates — review at 48–72 h and 5–7 days.
    • Duplicate therapy alerts — e.g., two drugs with overlapping spectra.
  4. Tracking & monitoring — antibiotic consumption (DDD/1000 patient-days); resistance patterns (antibiogram); C. difficile rates; clinical outcomes.
  5. Reporting — to prescribers, hospital administration, infection control committee.
  6. Education — regular training of medical, nursing, pharmacy staff.

Why AMSP Matters

  • Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) — >1.27 million deaths globally attributable to bacterial AMR in 2019 (Lancet); India has among the highest rates of multidrug-resistant organisms (MRSA, VRE, ESBL, CRE, CRAB, CRPA).
  • Misuse of antibiotics — ~50% of antibiotic prescriptions in hospitals are inappropriate (unnecessary, wrong drug, wrong dose, wrong duration).
  • Without effective antibiotics — chemotherapy, surgery, neonatal care, and transplantation become life-threatening.
  • WHO calls AMR one of the top 10 global public health threats.

Indian Context — ICMR AMSP

  • ICMR initiated AMSP network in 2017–2018; >150 hospitals enrolled.
  • Annual AMR surveillance reports — publish antibiograms.
  • "Red Line Campaign" — distinguishes prescription-only antibiotics (red line on packaging) from OTC.
  • National Action Plan on AMR (NAP-AMR, 2017–2021) — multi-sectoral "One Health" approach.

Clinical Pearl

The single most effective stewardship intervention is prospective audit & feedback — a pharmacist or ID physician reviews all antibiotic prescriptions after 48–72 h and recommends continuation, narrowing, switching to oral, or stopping. This reduces broad-spectrum antibiotic use by 20–30% without compromising outcomes. The second is pre-authorisation of last-resort antibiotics (carbapenems, colistin, linezolid, tigecycline) — approval by ID physician before dispensing. Always send cultures before starting antibiotics — this enables de-escalation from broad empiric to narrow targeted therapy within 48–72 h. The "Start Smart, Then Focus" approach (UK Department of Health) is the simplest bedside mnemonic — start with appropriate empiric therapy within 1 h of severe sepsis, then review at 48–72 h based on cultures and clinical response. Avoid antibiotics for viral upper respiratory infections — the single most common misuse of antibiotics in outpatient practice.

Definition

Cell-mediated immunity (CMI) is the arm of adaptive immunity mediated by T lymphocytes and other immune cells (rather than by antibodies). It defends against intracellular pathogens (viruses, intracellular bacteria — TB, Listeria, Salmonella; protozoa — Leishmania, Toxoplasma, Plasmodium; fungi — Candida, Histoplasma), malignant cells, and transplanted tissue. CMI is also responsible for Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity.

Cells Involved in CMI

1. T Lymphocytes — Central

  • CD4+ Helper T cells — recognise antigen presented on MHC class II by professional APCs (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells). Subsets:
    • Th1 — secrets IFN-γ, IL-2 — activates macrophages; defends against intracellular pathogens (TB, viruses); DTH. Transcription factor T-bet.
    • Th2 — secrets IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 — allergy, asthma, parasites; B cell help for IgE. GATA3.
    • Th17 — secrets IL-17, IL-22 — extracellular bacteria & fungi at mucosa; autoimmune inflammation. RORγt.
    • Tfh (follicular helper) — secrets IL-21 — germinal centre formation & B cell help. Bcl-6.
    • Treg (regulatory) — FoxP3+, IL-10, TGF-β — immune tolerance, suppresses effector T cells.
  • CD8+ Cytotoxic T Lymphocytes (CTLs) — recognise antigen presented on MHC class I (all nucleated cells); kill virus-infected, tumour, transplant cells via:
    • Perforin/granzyme — perforin creates pores; granzyme enters & activates caspases → apoptosis.
    • FasL-Fas — Fas ligand on CTL binds Fas (CD95) on target → caspase-8 → apoptosis.
    • Cytokines — IFN-γ, TNF-α, TNF-β — inhibit viral replication, recruit other immune cells.
  • γδ T cells — TCR γδ; MHC-independent; mucosal & skin intraepithelial; rapid cytokine response.
  • NKT cells — express NK markers + TCR; recognise lipid antigen on CD1d; rapid IFN-γ, IL-4.

2. Antigen-Presenting Cells (APCs)

  • Dendritic cells — most potent APC; bridge innate & adaptive; primary naïve T cell activator.
  • Macrophages — phagocytose; present antigen on MHC-II to effector/memory CD4+ T cells; activated by Th1 IFN-γ to kill intracellular pathogens.
  • B cells — antigen-specific uptake via BCR; present to CD4+ Tfh cells.

3. Effector Cells of CMI

  • Activated macrophages — enhanced phagocytosis, ROS/RNS production (respiratory burst, iNOS); granuloma formation.
  • NK cells — kill virus-infected & tumour cells (missing-self); ADCC via FcγRIII (CD16) binds IgG-coated target.
  • Eosinophils — parasite defence (MBP, ECP); allergy.

4. Cytokines

  • IL-2 (T cell proliferation); IFN-γ (macrophage activation, Th1); IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 (Th2); IL-17, IL-22 (Th17); IL-12 (Th1 polarisation); TNF-α (inflammation, granuloma); TGF-β (Treg, fibrosis, IgA switching); IL-10 (immunosuppression).

Mechanism of CMI

Phase 1 — Antigen Recognition & T Cell Priming

  1. Pathogen engulfed by dendritic cell → processed intracellularly → peptide loaded onto MHC class I (endogenous — viral/cytosolic proteins) or MHC class II (exogenous — phagolysosomal).
  2. Dendritic cell migrates to draining lymph node; matures (upregulates MHC, B7 co-stimulator, CCR7).
  3. Naïve T cell in lymph node paracortex recognises peptide-MHC via TCR (signal 1).
  4. Co-stimulation — CD28 on T cell binds B7 (CD80/86) on DC (signal 2) — essential for activation; without it, anergy.
  5. Cytokines from DC (IL-12 → Th1; IL-4 → Th2; IL-6 + TGF-β + IL-23 → Th17; IL-10 + TGF-β → Treg) polarise naïve T cell (signal 3).
  6. T cell proliferates 10⁴–10⁶-fold (clonal expansion, blast transformation); differentiates into effector & memory cells.

Phase 2 — Effector Function

  • CD4+ Th1 cells — migrate to site of infection; recognise antigen on macrophage MHC-II; release IFN-γ → activates macrophage → enhanced phagocytosis, ROS, RNS, granuloma formation; kills intracellular pathogens (TB, Listeria, Salmonella).
  • CD4+ Th17 cells — recruit neutrophils via IL-17 → extracellular bacteria & fungi.
  • CD8+ CTLs — migrate to infected tissue; recognise peptide-MHC I on infected cell; release perforin/granzyme → apoptosis; FasL-Fas; cytokines IFN-γ, TNF-α inhibit viral replication.
  • γδ T cells & NKT cells — rapid innate-like response; cytokine release.
  • NK cells — kill cells with downregulated MHC-I (virus, tumour); ADCC.

Phase 3 — Resolution & Memory

  • Effector cells undergo apoptosis (activation-induced cell death — AICD) as antigen cleared.
  • Memory T cells persist — central memory (TCM) in lymph nodes; effector memory (TEM) in tissues; resident memory (TRM) in epithelial barriers.
  • Memory response — faster, larger, higher affinity on re-exposure.

Functions of CMI

  • Defence against intracellular pathogens — viruses, TB, Listeria, Salmonella, Brucella, Leishmania, Toxoplasma, Plasmodium, fungi.
  • Tumour surveillance — CD8+ CTLs kill tumour cells; basis of cancer immunotherapy (checkpoint inhibitors — nivolumab anti-PD-1, ipilimumab anti-CTLA-4; CAR-T cell therapy).
  • Transplant rejection — host T cells recognise foreign MHC (alloreactivity); acute cellular rejection of solid organ transplant.
  • Graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) — donor T cells attack host tissues post-HSCT.
  • Type IV hypersensitivity — tuberculin skin test, contact dermatitis (poison ivy, nickel), granulomatous disease.
  • Autoimmunity — T cell-mediated tissue damage — type 1 diabetes (β-cell destruction), multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Hashimoto thyroiditis.

Assessment of CMI

  • Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) — DTH reaction; measures prior sensitisation to TB.
  • IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) — IFN-γ release assay; measures T cell response to TB antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10).
  • Flow cytometry — CD3, CD4, CD8 counts; CD4/CD8 ratio.
  • Lymphocyte proliferation assay — tritiated thymidine incorporation.
  • DCM (delayed cutaneous hypersensitivity) — Candida, mumps, tetanus antigens; anergy panel.

Examples of CMI Deficiency

  • DiGeorge syndrome — thymic aplasia; T cell deficiency.
  • SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency) — T + B cell defect.
  • HIV/AIDS — CD4+ T cell depletion; opportunistic infections (PJP, Toxoplasma, CMV, MAC, Cryptococcus); Kaposi sarcoma.
  • Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis — IL-17 pathway defects (STAT1, AIRE — APECED).
  • IFN-γ pathway defects — disseminated BCG, environmental mycobacteria, Salmonella.

Clinical Pearl

The thymus is essential for T cell development — DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion, CATCH-22) causes thymic aplasia → absent T cells → severe viral, fungal, and intracellular bacterial infections; if untreated, fatal in infancy. Thymic transplantation can rescue. The CD4 count is the most important laboratory marker in HIV — guides when to start ART (<500 cells/µL per WHO; <350 cells/µL symptomatic; <200 cells/µL requires PCP prophylaxis with TMP-SMX; <100 cells/µL requires MAC prophylaxis with azithromycin; <50 cells/µL requires CMV surveillance). Granuloma formation (TB, sarcoidosis, fungal, foreign body) is the hallmark of intense Th1-mediated CMI — epithelioid macrophages & multinucleated giant cells surround the pathogen, containing it. Checkpoint inhibitor cancer therapy (nivolumab anti-PD-1, ipilimumab anti-CTLA-4) unleashes pre-existing anti-tumour CD8+ T cells — has revolutionised melanoma, lung, and renal cancer treatment, but causes immune-related adverse events (colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathy) — because the brake is removed from self-reactive T cells too.
